stories.title: South Korea's 8.4GW AI data center buildout faces internal power design bottleneck
stories.summary: South Korea is pushing ahead with plans for roughly 8.4GW of AI data center capacity, but internal power design and cooling constraints are emerging as key bottlenecks. Industry observers warn that grid limitations and facility-level engineering hurdles could slow the buildout.
stories.why_it_matters: The gap between announced capacity and deliverable power is becoming the defining constraint on Korea's AI infrastructure ambitions. Developers, utilities, and equipment suppliers all face pressure to resolve power distribution and cooling design issues before projects can move from announcement to operation.
stories.content:
![South Korea's 8.4GW AI Data Center Buildout Faces Biggest Bottleneck in Internal Power Design](https://img.biggo.com/_6T4MZZpYKd9q-mT_TeQLxd8zEkm4AI7g9u2YeyDriw/fit/1720/0/sm/0/aHR0cHM6Ly9pbWcuYmdvLm9uZS9uZXdzLWltYWdlL2FpX2dlbmVyYXRlZC8yMDI2LTA4L2E5ZWI2ZTFiLTQ1N2EtNDllZS1hZjIyLTEzNzFjOGUyNjgyZF8xNzg3NDM3ODk1X2RlZmF1bHQuanBn.webp)

The South Korean government's announcement that it will build 8.4 gigawatts (GW) of artificial intelligence (AI) data center capacity by 2029 has made power procurement the central challenge. Experts say the bottleneck lies not only in where and how electricity is sourced, but also in how that power is distributed and cooled once inside the data center.

In June, the government unveiled its "Three Mega Projects for South Korea's Great Leap Forward," committing to a first phase of 8.4GW of AI data center capacity, including 5GW from SK, 2.4GW from GS, and 1GW from Naver. The long-term plan calls for expanding total capacity to 18.4GW, with support for power and water supply, site diversification, and demonstration of South Korean-made power and cooling solutions.

What sets AI data centers apart from conventional ones is the rapid escalation in power draw per server rack. A server rack is a bundle of servers containing GPUs, central processing units (CPUs), memory, and storage. Under existing low-voltage power architectures, as rack power grows, so do current, heat, and power-loss burdens. This is why observers argue that both the external grid running from power plants to the data center and the internal power delivery path from the data center to the GPU—the so-called "electric highway"—must be validated together.

### The 1MW-per-Rack Era and the Limits of 48V Architecture

Lee Jeong-ho, a professor of mechanical engineering at Ajou University, said, "These days Nvidia doesn't sell GPU chips one by one—it sells them as racks. Current AI server racks draw roughly 150kW, the next generation will reach 600kW, and in the long term a single rack could scale to 1MW."

The 48V power architecture widely used in server racks today offers the advantages of familiarity and safety due to its low voltage. But when transmitting the same amount of power, lower voltage means higher current. Supplying 100kW to a single rack requires more than 2,000 amps under a 48V design. As rack power grows to 600kW and 1MW, even greater current is needed, compounding wiring, thermal, and power-loss burdens.

A paper published last month on the preprint server arXiv flagged the same issue. An international research team including Lee Sang-hwi, a professor at Korea University, analyzed how the growth in AI workloads is increasing data center power demand, instantaneous current swings, and thermal stress, and concluded that the existing 48V server rack architecture and low-voltage AC distribution could hit their limits.

The researchers proposed alternatives including raising intra-rack voltage to 400V or 800V, shifting data center internal distribution to a DC-centric model, and connecting the grid to the data center via medium-voltage solid-state transformers. Solid-state transformers use more power electronics than conventional transformers to finely control voltage conversion and power flow. Higher voltage allows the same power to be delivered at lower current, while DC distribution reduces conversion stages and cuts losses.

However, these design shifts still require further research and demonstration. Because data centers must run around the clock without interruption, deploying high-voltage DC distribution demands validation of where to interrupt power during faults, how to prevent electric shock and fire, how to handle grounding, and whether the system remains stable over long-term operation. The researchers themselves identified protection and fault response, grounding, standardization, long-term reliability, co-design of thermal and electrical systems, and digital twin-based verification as the key bottlenecks for next-generation power architectures.

### Cooling Technology Must Be Redesigned in Tandem

When the electric highway of an AI data center changes, thermal management must change with it, because a substantial share of GPU power consumption is converted to heat. Professor Lee explained, "GPUs generally need to operate below roughly 85 degrees Celsius to deliver full performance, and as power consumption rises, so does heat. It's the same principle as a phone getting hot after prolonged use."

Conventional data centers have primarily relied on air cooling, blowing cold air into server rooms to extract heat. But as AI server power draw climbs, the center of gravity in cooling is shifting from air to liquid. Liquid cooling circulates water or dielectric coolant close to the chip to remove heat, transferring it far more efficiently than air.

As next-generation AI chips consume even more power, cooling devices must move closer to the chip—and ultimately inside the chip or semiconductor package. Kim Sung-jin, a professor of mechanical engineering at KAIST, said, "Liquid cooling is already in use, but companies like Intel and HP are developing technologies to embed cooling devices inside the chip itself. The technology isn't mature yet, so it will take time. Integrating multiple chips and cooling devices at scale is not easy."

Whether South Korea can actually validate new power delivery and cooling architectures is another variable. An AI data center is not a facility where server racks, power supplies, and cooling units can be swapped out independently. Power delivery and cooling hardware are attached according to the rack architecture defined by the server manufacturer.

Professor Lee Jeong-ho said, "South Korea says it's building AI data centers, but the core is missing. We can produce the component technologies needed for cooling, but there is no company in South Korea that builds complete systems or server and rack technology." He added, "Even if we actually set up an AI data center, it is nearly impossible right now to configure it the way we want."

### External Grid and Transmission Timelines Are Also Wild Cards

The power grid challenges outside the AI data center remain as well. Researchers at the University of Calgary in Canada have analyzed how the rapid proliferation of AI data centers amplifies not just total power demand but also issues of location, timing, and power variability. If data center loads concentrate in specific regions, they could outpace the expansion of clean energy, while grid flexibility, reliability, and carbon emissions concerns grow in tandem.

Lee Yu-soo, a professor in the Department of Energy Policy and Technology Convergence at Soongsil University, also cautioned that plans to use renewable energy from South Korea's Honam region for AI data centers should be viewed carefully. "AI training workloads require large-scale GPUs running simultaneously, so power must be supplied stably 24 hours a day," he said. "It won't be easy unless renewable energy is combined with sources like nuclear or liquefied natural gas (LNG)."

Transmission grid construction speed is another variable. Professor Lee said, "South Korea has many long-distance transmission arrangements from power plants, so the pace of transmission grid construction is critical. Transmission projects come with community acceptance issues, costs, and schedule delays." He added, "It's uncertain whether data center commissioning and power supply timelines will align. The whole picture needs to be re-examined."

arXiv paper DOIs: https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2606.25095, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2606.21064

stories.title: Korean engineers turn to the deep sea for data centers
stories.summary: South Korean engineers are exploring underwater data center concepts, placing facilities in the deep sea as a way to address cooling and land constraints. The approach follows similar experiments by Microsoft and others with submerged server deployments.
stories.why_it_matters: If viable, subsea facilities could ease two of Korea's most pressing data center constraints at once — land scarcity and cooling costs. The research positions Korean engineering firms at the front of an experimental deployment model that, if proven, could alter site-selection economics across coastal APAC markets.
stories.content:
A small Korean coastal city could soon host up to 100,000 AI servers

![Data center](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/kntXJzuBjvVTZvqgBeCKfN.jpg) 

- **Ulsan is testing underwater data centers to support growing AI workloads**
- **The project carries a KRW 51.1 billion (about $37 million) budget through 2030**
- **Seawater could provide cooling without conventional mechanical refrigeration systems**

South Korean city Ulsan is exploring underwater infrastructure as AI computing continues to strain land availability, power grids, and cooling systems nationwide.

The city is partnering with the Korea Institute of Ocean Science and Technology (KIOST) to design a standardized subsea data center model.

Officials hope the approach can ease some of the site and cooling constraints that conventional data centers increasingly face across the country.

## Building a standardized underwater model

The partnership between Ulsan and KIOST runs through 2030, with a combined budget of KRW 51.1 billion (about $37 million) - KRW 40 billion (about $29 million) of which comes directly from the central government, with the remainder covered locally.

“Ulsan plans to complete the standard model by 2030 and begin developing an underwater data-center complex for commercialization from 2031,” the city said.

The goal is a working, carbon-neutral template for underwater computing that other sites could later replicate.

The project will take place in waters roughly 20 meters deep off the Ulsan coastline, where engineers plan to rely on seawater — which averages about 13.3°C annually — as a core part of the cooling strategy.

Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!

Researchers intend to combine pressure-resistant vessel design with hybrid cooling systems described as ultra-high-efficiency by project planners.

Server units and power distribution equipment will follow standardized modular designs meant to simplify future scaling.

The team is aiming for an operating efficiency of approximately PUE 1.2 once testing concludes.

SK Telecom joined the partnership in January 2026, taking on responsibility for GPU-based infrastructure and server operations management.

In addition to Ulsan and KIOST, other research organizations, academics and industry professionals are part of the project working behind the scenes.

Their combined role covers everything from vessel engineering to the software layer that will eventually manage AI workloads underwater.

## A larger commercial vision

A separate, longer-term concept discussed by the city involves roughly KRW 500 billion (about $360 million) in investment and capacity for up to 100,000 servers.

This larger sum is not tied to the current phase of work and only reflects what a full commercial buildout could eventually cost.

Whether Ulsan reaches that scale will depend entirely on how the initial testing phase performs.

South Korea faces mounting pressure to expand computing capacity as AI workloads multiply across chipmakers, cloud providers, and research institutions nationwide.

Land near major population centers remains scarce and expensive, pushing planners toward unconventional sites away from crowded urban areas.

Ocean water offers a cooling resource that requires none of the mechanical refrigeration conventional facilities depend on heavily.

If the Ulsan demonstration performs as expected, similar underwater sites could eventually spread along other stretches of Korea's coastline.

For now, the ocean floor represents a promising but unproven answer to Korea's expanding AI infrastructure demands.

stories.title: What coolant should you use for data center liquid cooling? (Sponsored)
stories.summary: This sponsored article examines coolant options for data center liquid cooling, comparing PG25, dielectric fluids, and other chemistries against ASHRAE recommendations. It outlines the trade-offs operators face when selecting fluids for direct-to-chip or immersion systems.
stories.why_it_matters: As liquid cooling moves from niche to mainstream in high-density AI facilities, coolant choice is becoming a procurement and compliance decision with long-term operational consequences. Operators need clear guidance on standards alignment to avoid locking in fluids that create safety, warranty, or environmental liabilities.
stories.content:
There’s little question that AI data centers require liquid cooling, as AI workloads drive ever-increasing rack densities. So, coolant selection, fluid management, and cooling system reliability all become paramount. It’s natural, then, that questions arise about the most common cooling fluid, PG25, as well as what ASHRAE and the Open Compute Project (OCP) recommend.

In this blog post, I’ll tackle some of the most common coolant questions we hear from hyperscalers, colocation providers, neoclouds, and other data center ecosystem players.

Let’s start with a basic question: What coolant should I use for data center liquid cooling?

Companies have three main fluid options for liquid data center cooling: dielectrics, deionized water plus additives, and PG25. Dielectrics are used mainly for immersion cooling, which really can’t keep up with the increasing cooling requirements of AI chips.

Deionized (DI) water performs well, but the maintenance required to keep the fluid clean can significantly increase costs. The industry has thus settled on PG25, which performs nearly as well as DI water but with far less fluid maintenance.

![Decision-making-e1621619175850-1024x619-1](https://media.datacenterdynamics.com/media/images/Decision-making-e1621619175850-1024x619-1.width-880.jpg) 

## What is PG25 coolant for data centers?

PG25 is a mix of 75 percent water and 25 percent propylene glycol (PG). At a 25 percent concentration, PG inhibits bio growth. Interestingly, at 10 percent, algae and other biomatter tend to feed on PG, but 25 percent is the sweet spot at which the solution becomes biostatic, meaning it inhibits growth.

PG25 also generally includes other additives to further prevent bacterial growth and corrosion in the copper within coolant distribution units (CDUs) and cold plates that carry the fluid.

Each fluid manufacturer has its own secret sauce in terms of the exact formulation, but the main goals are to prevent corrosion and bio-growth. That’s important because the cold plates have tight fin spacing, around 50 microns wide today with future cold plates possibly going even tighter.

Any growth on those plates can affect cooling performance, cause thermal throttling, and potentially damage the expensive IT equipment. So, it’s imperative to prevent growth of algae or any other biological fouling. As an added benefit, PG25 offers freeze protection down to about -10°C (14°F).

## What does ASHRAE recommend for liquid cooling fluids?

ASHRAE doesn’t generally make recommendations. It does write standards, but they’re not mandates. That said, they do have groups that look at issues like data center cooling, namely Technical Committee 9.9 (TC 9.9), for Mission Critical Facilities, Data Centers, Technology Spaces, and Electronic Equipment.

Many of the players working within ASHRAE to guide data center design are involved with TC 9.9, as well as ANSI/ASHRAE Standard 90.4, which is the main standard covering data center efficiency. While that standard doesn’t recommend any specific fluid, it mainly focuses on PG25 and DI water.

## What is the OCP coolant standard?

Unlike ASHRAE, OCP does make recommendations, with the goal of providing a framework for the data center industry to deploy liquid cooling at scale quickly and safely. OCP recommends PG25 because it solves the problems previously identified in this blog post.

## How often should I test coolant in a data center CDU loop?

This question gets to cooling chemistry, which does affect liquid cooling reliability. If your fluid performance starts to degrade, it may lead to issues including biological growth, corrosion, scale formation, and more – all of which can ultimately lead to IT equipment problems. Testing can help you detect fluid failures and correct them before algae has a chance to grow.

Think about testing with a tiered approach. For a brand new, just-commissioned system, you want to test daily or even multiple times per day. The idea is to catch any initial changes in fluid chemistry that may have a detrimental effect, such as a drop in the PG concentration.

It’s not uncommon for concentrations to change significantly as the fluid makes its first pass through the CDU as it mixes with residual flushing DI water that may not have been removed fully. It’s not difficult to boost the concentration, such as by adding a PG50 solution, but you need to test to determine if that’s required.

After a week or so, or whenever your testing shows the fluid concentration has stabilized, you can shift to weekly sampling. Now you’re starting to run jobs on your IT equipment, so you need to monitor how fluid concentrations change under load.

Here again, once you see stability, you can shift to a less-frequent schedule, perhaps monthly. The exact frequency depends on the facility and the balance you want to strike between risk and cost.

## When should I use propylene glycol versus ethylene glycol?

The short answer here is, in the vast majority of cases, use PG25. Ethylene glycol (EG) has somewhat better thermal performance and lower viscosity than PG, but it’s far more toxic to humans. For that reason, it’s seldom used in data centers. It’s more often used for freeze protection in automotive applications, such as your car’s cooling system, or in other closed-loop HVAC applications where humans generally don’t need to touch it.

In an IT environment, you will need to disconnect the fluid loops each time you swap out a server blade, which happens frequently during server maintenance. During servicing, the quick disconnects (QDs) often have a slightly wetted disconnect rather than a 100 percent dry break. PG25 is perfectly safe in that situation; EG is not.

## Coolant selection for data center liquid cooling: From selection to management

As AI pushes rack densities and chip power higher, liquid cooling strategies are becoming increasingly important, and choosing the right coolant is a key part of that strategy. The right fluid, combined with regular testing, proactive management, and the right architecture, can help improve cooling performance and reliability while protecting AI infrastructure and major investments over the long term.

stories.title: Building data centers is getting easier. Building trust is not
stories.summary: This commentary argues that while data center construction has become more streamlined, earning community trust has not kept pace. It urges operators to stop treating local communities as an afterthought in project development.
stories.why_it_matters: Community opposition is emerging as a real schedule and permitting risk for data center projects, particularly as facilities scale into power-hungry AI campuses near populated areas. Developers that invest early in local engagement stand to protect timelines and social license, while those that don't face delays, litigation, and moratoria.
stories.content:
In the Lammermuir Hills of the Scottish Borders, a developer is proposing to build three data center buildings, each up to 24 meters tall, on land where the loudest sound has typically been wind. The £2 billion ($2.7bn) investment project is still in the pre-application phase, but it has already prompted a 10,000-signatures-strong public petition and organized local opposition.

This is increasingly the opening chapter for hyperscale developments around the world: a proposal, followed by resistance, followed by delays that often prove harder to overcome than the engineering itself.

AI is driving an unprecedented need for compute capacity, while governments increasingly view digital infrastructure as a strategic asset rather than simply another real estate class. Analysts expect global demand for data center capacity to continue rising sharply over the remainder of the decade, fueled largely by AI workloads. Meeting that demand will require new facilities at a scale the industry has never attempted before.

For many communities, that investment brings genuine opportunity. Large-scale developments create construction jobs, attract long-term capital and support local businesses throughout the supply chain. Regions that have experienced decades of industrial decline can benefit from a new generation of infrastructure investment, while operational facilities create skilled technical roles that contribute to local economies long after construction has finished.

Yet those benefits do not erase legitimate concerns.

The same qualities that make a site attractive to a developer — open land, available power, a quiet setting — are exactly what a nearby community values about the place it lives. Construction on a hyperscale campus runs for years, not months, and the noise carries. Landscapes change dramatically. Facilities consume significant amounts of electricity and, depending on their design, substantial volumes of water. Residents naturally ask whether local infrastructure will come under pressure and whether the character of their area will be permanently altered.

These are just some of the specific, recurring reasons opposition keeps forming around new projects, and they show up again and again once a proposal becomes public.

Outside Melbourne, Australia, local communities have objected to the expansion of a hyperscale campus, citing prolonged construction noise and plans to increase the site's backup diesel generators. In Inzai, near Tokyo, residents have sued the private inspection company that approved a 52-meter data center planned next door, seeking to have the building permit nullified.

All over the world, we’re seeing the same underlying pattern: a project moves forward on its own timeline until it collides with a community that was never meaningfully part of the conversation.

The industry should resist the temptation to dismiss this as simple resistance to progress. Most people understand the importance of digital infrastructure: every cloud application, online transaction, and AI model depends on facilities like these, and few would argue that we need fewer data centers.

The question is whether we are building them in a way that earns public confidence, and too often, communities feel the answer is *no.*

For developers and investors alike, community engagement needs to be treated as an essential part of project delivery, because the cost of getting this wrong extends well beyond public relations.

Delayed approvals, legal challenges and prolonged planning disputes create uncertainty for investors, increase project costs and slow the delivery of infrastructure that markets urgently need. In an industry where access to power, land and grid capacity is already constrained, losing months or even years because of avoidable community opposition is an increasingly expensive mistake, but an avoidable one.

Fixing it starts with transparency and building trust. Communities deserve clear information about what is being built, why a site has been selected, and how disruption during construction will be managed. Engagement should begin before positions become entrenched, not after opposition has already formed.

It also means recognizing that every community has different priorities. In one location, water consumption may be the dominant concern. Elsewhere, it may be visual impact, traffic or noise — a standardized consultation process is unlikely to address issues that are inherently local.

Environmental performance also matters, not simply because regulators expect it, but because communities increasingly do. Operators are investing in more efficient cooling technologies, renewable energy procurement, closed-loop water systems and waste heat recovery. These measures improve operational efficiency, but they also demonstrate that developers are taking local concerns seriously rather than asking communities to accept disruption in exchange for promises of future economic benefit.

Finally, developers should think beyond the site boundary.

The strongest projects create lasting relationships with the communities around them through local hiring, skills partnerships with colleges and universities, investment in supporting infrastructure and procurement opportunities for regional businesses. These initiatives can help ensure that the economic benefits of a project are visible to the people living alongside it.

As more capacity competes for a shrinking pool of sites with adequate power, land, and water, the developers who have already built local trust will have first pick of the remaining good ground, while the ones who have not will find every subsequent application slower and more expensive than the last.

Data centers are long-term assets whose value is measured over decades, not planning cycles. Projects that establish strong relationships with local communities are often better positioned to expand, adapt and operate successfully throughout their lifespan. Those that fail to do so may secure planning permission, but they inherit a more difficult operating environment from day one.

Data centers are long-term assets. Let’s not forget that communities are too.

stories.title: Powering data centers is no longer a simple matter of supply and demand (Sponsored)
stories.summary: In this sponsored piece, Ramboll's Michael Bergstrom argues that powering data centers has moved beyond simple supply-and-demand dynamics. Unprecedented load growth, evolving grid standards, and shifting utility requirements are reshaping the data center development lifecycle.
stories.why_it_matters: Developers can no longer treat power procurement as a late-stage checklist item; utility engagement now shapes site selection, timelines, and project viability from day one. Firms that fail to adapt their planning processes risk stranded capital in markets where grid access has become the gating factor.
stories.content:
Data center facilities are no longer small, isolated sites with simple power demands but critical infrastructure projects that now require multi-gigawatt campuses to match the rising demand. Consequently, securing power has evolved into a complex engineering and regulatory challenge.

In this DCD>Talks episode, Michael Bergstrom, senior manager of energy market development at Ramboll, outlines how unprecedented load growth, changing grid standards, and shifting utility requirements are transforming the project lifecycle.

From physically climbing over 100 wind turbines early in his career to now guiding clients through grid access, on-site generation, and waste heat recovery, Bergstrom leverages his wide experience across industries to help facilities navigate an increasingly tight power grid.

This diverse background offers a unique vantage point on the evolving sector where power is no longer just a supply problem, but a multi-layered hurdle across design, grid modeling, and utility collaboration.

## The end of passive interconnection

For decades, electricity demand across North America remained relatively flat. The rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence and hyperscale infrastructure changed that balance in the last few years, placing intense pressure on aging utility infrastructure.

Previously, developers could enter interconnection queues with aspirational targets or vague expansion timelines. Today, utilities and regional transmission organizations demand highly specific technical details from day one.

“Upfront, you really need to have a specific load profile for the data center that you’re going to build – ideally matching up with a specific tenant or operator. Because data center loads can move up and down quite quickly, having those plans in place as soon as you speak to a utility is really important,” says Bergstrom.

Without concrete operational models, developers risk being stalled in increasingly competitive interconnection queues.

## Meeting stricter grid compliance

As data centers introduce massive, volatile loads to local networks, grid operators are tightening reliability criteria. Issues like subsynchronous frequency oscillations – which can threaten grid stability – are moving from niche technical considerations to mandatory compliance factors.

To mitigate these disruptions, developers are increasingly integrating advanced hardware directly at the substation level. Bergstrom notes:

“Grid compliance standards are changing. They are becoming more stringent. We’re going to see an increased use for technologies like battery energy storage systems and statcoms at the grid level to handle dynamic responses to reactive power.”

Advanced power modeling and site-level stabilization tools are fast becoming a prerequisite for securing utility approvals. According to him, these technologies are going to be more standard, if not almost required, moving forward across large sites.

## Speed to power vs. project viability

While the industry-wide rush for rapid power access continues, the definition of “speed to power” is shifting. Merely holding a power reservation is no longer enough to guarantee a viable development. Bergstrom explains:

“It’s not just access to power; it’s access to an implementable project. That’s where having plans in place – where you understand interconnection, community engagement, and permitting – ensures that when you do have power, the project is actually ready to move forward.”

Instead of relying solely on greenfield sites, many operators are pivoting toward scaling existing campuses to meet growing capacity needs without starting from scratch.

“We’re seeing a shift where developers are taking sites that were originally planned for hundreds of megawatts and looking at how to scale those into gigawatt-scale campuses,” he observes.

This strategy allows teams to leverage established infrastructure while solving complex Phase II power requirements, such as bridging power or behind-the-meter generation.

## Giving due diligence

To navigate these moving parts, early-stage site selection requires a much deeper level of scrutiny than in previous years. Simple proximity mapping to high-voltage transmission lines no longer provides a complete picture of feasibility as Bergstrom says:

“A few years ago, you could maybe just take a look on the map, do some GIS work, and see how close you are to large transmission lines. But that process has changed. You have to start upfront with power due diligence early in the process and make sure you’re actually going to have a pathway to power via pure grid interconnection, on-site generation, bridging power, or some hybrid solution.”

Integrated due diligence must weigh grid access alongside water availability, fiber connectivity, environmental impacts, and local community expectations simultaneously.

“You want to make sure that you’ve done your diligence properly, you know what your potential end users are looking for, and you’re matching those things up as much as you can in the beginning of the process and front-load it, so to speak.”

Addressing these technical constraints early is the single most effective way to protect project timelines and hit sustainability goals.

stories.title: NVIDIA invests $1 billion in NAVER to expand South Korea AI data center capacity
stories.summary: NVIDIA has committed a $1 billion investment in South Korean tech company NAVER to expand AI data center capacity in the country. The deal deepens ties between the chipmaker and one of Korea's leading cloud and AI platform operators.
stories.why_it_matters: The investment accelerates South Korea's bid to become a regional AI compute hub and gives NAVER the capital and hardware alignment to scale sovereign AI infrastructure. For the broader APAC market, it signals that chip vendors are increasingly willing to fund capacity buildouts directly, reshaping how large AI data center projects get financed.
stories.content:
source on Google

Nvidia Corp invests $1 billion in NAVER Corp via share issuance to expand the GAK Sejong AI datacenter to 200 megawatts by 2028. Nvidia will supply GPUs for the facility, with Brookfield Asset Management proposing up to $9 billion in additional funding. The deal follows previous partnerships with SK Hynix and SK Telecom, strengthening Nvidia's AI ecosystem in South Korea.

![46681894](http://news-images.dhan.co/nvidia-invests-1-billion-in-naver-to-expand-south-korea-ai-datacenter-capacity.jpg)

*this image is generated using AI for illustrative purposes only.

Nvidia Corp has agreed to invest approximately $1 billion in NAVER Corp, marking a significant expansion of its artificial intelligence footprint in South Korea. Announced on Saturday during South Korean President Lee Jae Myung’s visit to the AI Summit in San Francisco, the deal aims to scale up local AI computing capacity. The investment will see Nvidia acquire 7.2 million newly issued shares of NAVER at 204,500 KRW ($139.45) per share, representing a roughly 1% discount to NAVER’s Friday closing price.

The capital injection is primarily directed toward expanding NAVER’s GAK Sejong AI datacenter. The facility’s capacity is set to grow from 55 megawatts to 200 megawatts by 2028. In a regulatory filing on Monday, NAVER clarified the partnership structure, noting that Nvidia will participate as a supplier of GPUs rather than as an equity partner sharing revenue and business risks. This structural adjustment defines Nvidia’s role strictly within the hardware supply chain for the expanded infrastructure.

Brookfield Asset Management Ltd is also involved in the broader infrastructure push, proposing up to $9 billion to fund the AI infrastructure development. This substantial financial backing underscores the scale of the upcoming deployment. The expanded facility is expected to deploy next-generation Vera Rubin and Blackwell systems, providing production-scale AI computing capacity for enterprises, startups, and government organizations across the region.

This transaction builds upon a partnership announced in June, where NAVER committed to using Nvidia technology for AI data center expansion and industrial AI applications. That earlier announcement also highlighted Nvidia’s broader ecosystem partnerships in South Korea with SK Hynix, SK Telecom, and Doosan. The current deal solidifies Nvidia’s strategic position in the country’s rapidly growing AI sector.

Market reaction reflected the positive sentiment surrounding the deal. In Seoul, NAVER shares rose 7.23% to 222,500 KRW ($151.76) at the time of writing. Meanwhile, Nvidia’s shares closed 0.92% lower on Friday at $206.84, dipping another 0.02% in extended trading. The divergence in immediate stock performance highlights the distinct market dynamics affecting each entity despite the collaborative nature of the announcement.

## What the Numbers Show

The shift in partnership structure is a critical detail for investors analyzing Nvidia’s exposure in Asia. By moving from a risk-sharing partner model to a pure GPU supplier role, Nvidia secures high-margin hardware sales while limiting its operational liability in the datacenter’s long-term performance. The $1 billion equity stake ensures alignment with NAVER’s success, but the primary revenue driver will likely be the volume of Vera Rubin and Blackwell systems deployed in the 200-megawatt facility. With Brookfield proposing up to $9 billion in additional funding, the total capital pool for this single regional initiative suggests a massive scale of infrastructure development, potentially setting a template for future AI hub expansions in other Asian markets.
